Balanced forces and net force:
A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N). It has a size and a direction. The net force is the sum of all forces on an object. Forces in the same direction add. Forces in opposite directions subtract, and the net force points the way of the larger force.

Forces are balanced when the net force is 0 N. Then the motion does not change: an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps its velocity. Unbalanced forces change the speed or the direction of an object.
Newton's first and second laws:
First law: an object keeps its state of rest or its constant velocity unless an unbalanced force acts on it. This tendency is called inertia, and mass is the measure of inertia.

Second law: acceleration is proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass. The formula is F = m × a, with F in newtons, m in kilograms, and a in m/s^2. One newton is 1 kg × m/s^2. The acceleration has the same direction as the net force.
Newton's third law:
Third law: when object A pushes on object B, object B pushes back on A with a force equal in size and opposite in direction. These two forces are called an action-reaction pair.

The two forces of a pair act on different objects, so they never cancel each other. They are the same type of force and exist at the same time. Equal forces can give different accelerations, because a = F / m. Examples are a swimmer pushing water, a rocket and its exhaust gas, and walking.
Common types of forces:
Weight is the force of gravity on an object: W = m × g, with g about 10 N/kg on Earth and about 1.6 N/kg on the Moon. Mass stays the same everywhere, but weight changes. The normal force is the push of a surface on an object, perpendicular to the surface.

Friction opposes sliding between surfaces. Spring force tries to return a spring to its original length. Air resistance grows with speed and area. Gravity, magnetic and electric forces act at a distance.
